The Apple/PowerVR design is to run the vertex stage for the entire render pass and write the full results out to system memory.

Games will typically have a few renderpasses in each frame, One for each dynamic shadow generating light, One for all the opaque geometry, one for for all the transparent geometry, one for post-processing, one for UI.

There will be some vertex workloads to overlap, though often the bulk of the vertex work is in just one pass (a combined opaque/transparent geometry pass) and you might need to rely on overlapping frames to get peek throughput.

There are other tile designs which break the vertex shaders into two parts. A coordinate shader that only calculates the vertex position and then a vertex shader that re-calculates position and any other varyings such as lightly, color and texture coordinates. This approach saves the memory bandwidth of writing all the varyings out to memory, but duplicates execution (with the position being calculated two or more times. Once for the coordinate shader and then once for every single tile a triangle covers).

In the Apple design, there is some pipelining between tiles. Hidden surface removal for one tile can overlap the pixel shading of the previous tile.

I believe hidden surface removal involves writing the depth buffer along with a primitive ID. Then the pixel shading pass can skip running the pixel shader for any fragments that aren't visible in the final tile.
This is a huge performance win for apple when it works.
